Subject: Invoice question: April usage minimums & mixed call types

Hi Mateo,

Quick question on the latest invoice we received (April): we see two line items that look related to 'minimums / rounding' but the way short API calls (single-turn) and streaming sessions were aggregated seems unexpected. Specifically: 

- A block charge labeled 'mini-session floor (x10 tokens)' that appears to apply to a set of short, intermittent requests.
- A separate streaming bucket applied to the same day which seems to have been billed at full-seat minimum rather than prorated because there were only a few 30s streaming sessions.

Can you help explain how those two things are being atomized and whether they should have been coalesced (i.e., short calls absorbed into a streaming bucket or vice versa)? We're trying to reconcile to our internal usage and it's looking like double-counting of minimums for April 7th and 8th.

If helpful, I can share sample request-ids. We are under the LUM-8421 commitment.

Thanks — Emma
Emma Caldwell
Head of Platform Integrations, Lumina Health

From: mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>

Hi Emma — thanks for flagging this and sending the snippet. I ran the line items through our billing playbook and here's a short explanation plus next steps. TL;DR: you were billed for two separate minimums because the traffic matched two distinct billing atoms (short-call quantum vs streaming minimum) and our aggregation rules didn't coalesce them in this instance.

What happened (short answer):
- Our metering distinguishes "per-call" mini-sessions (used for short, stateless API calls) from "streaming sessions". Each has its own minimum unit: mini-session floor (default 10 tokens) and streaming seat-minute (default minute granularity).
- On April 7–8 the account generated ~520 short calls (many <50 tokens) and 6 streaming sessions that were <= 2 minutes each. Because these were not contiguous (different Request-IDs and different routing policies), the system applied the mini-session floor to the short calls and applied streaming minimums independently.

Why they didn't coalesce:
- Coalescing requires a shared context-id or KV-cache reuse within a 5 minute window (our default prefix affinity window). The short calls here used ephemeral request tokens (no persistent context-id), so they are considered separate atoms.
- The streaming sessions were routed to a different serving pool (optimized for low-latency streaming) and not eligible for bundling into the mini-session bucket.

Sample calc (attached):
- Short calls: 520 calls x effective floor 10 tokens = 5,200 tokens billed under "mini-session floors"
- Streaming: 6 sessions x 1-minute minimum x streaming seat-rate = 6 seat-minutes billed
- Effective double-minimum on Apr 7–8 = approximately 0.9% of monthly bill (we know any number looks bad; still small but we understand it matters).

I've attached a quick spreadsheet (mini_invoice_breakdown.xlsx) with per-request examples and how the atoms were applied. If you'd like, we can: 
1) Run a one-off reconciliation to see whether those short calls could be reclassified to a streaming bucket (requires matching request-ids / session cookies).
2) Offer a one-time rounding concession if reconciliation isn't practical.

Next steps — what I need from you:
- If you can share 5–10 request-ids for April 7–8, I can run the reclassify job and confirm whether coalescing would have changed the billing.
- If not, say so and I'll loop in Billing for a one-time concession (keeps things moving).

Thanks,
Mateo Alvarez
Account Executive — Redwood Inference
[Attachment: mini_invoice_breakdown.xlsx (calc spreadsheet)]

Two possible remediation paths: reclassify a subset of short calls into streaming (if they tie to session ids) or offer a one-time concession equal to the rounding delta.

Key facts:
- Short-call floors: ~5,200 tokens billed (aggregation of 520 calls at 10-token floor)
- Streaming minimums: 6 seat-minutes billed (sessions were short; routing separated pools)
- Estimated overcharge (if coalescing was technically appropriate): ~$1,120 USD (0.9% of month's bill) — see spreadsheet.

Ask:
- Can Billing run a quick reclassify check (script: billing/reclassify_by_requestid) if customer provides 5–10 request-ids? That would confirm whether coalescing would be legitimate.
- If customer can't provide ids, are we comfortable offering a one-time credit for the rounding difference (we've done this previously for partner goodwill)?

Triage recommendation: prioritize the reconciliation attempt first (keeps bookkeeping clean). If customer cannot produce ids in 48 hours, approve a one-time credit and I'll send an adjustment notice.
